opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So when I talk about annotation 2.0, I'm really reacting to how we've done things for the last decade or so. Annotation 1.0 was essentially: collect a big pile of data, ship it off to a large workforce, and have people draw boxes or polygons on everything, frame by frame, from scratch. It was expensive, it was slow, and frankly a lot of that human effort was spent on the easy cases that a model could already handle.

The transition I see is a shift in where the human sits in the loop. With today's foundation models, open-vocabulary detectors, segmentation models, vision-language models, we can generate a reasonable first pass of labels automatically, often at a fraction of the cost. So the human's role moves from *creating* every label to *curating and verifying* them. You spend your attention on the hard cases: the ambiguous examples, the rare classes, the places where the model is uncertain or where two models disagree.

That changes the workflow in a few important ways. First, annotation becomes much more tightly coupled to data understanding. Before you label anything, you want to explore the dataset, look at embeddings, find duplicates, find gaps, figure out what's actually worth labeling. Second, quality becomes the central question rather than quantity. If you're auto-labeling millions of samples, you need good ways to measure and find label errors, because a systematic mistake from the auto-labeler can propagate everywhere. And third, it's iterative. You label, you train, you evaluate, you look at where the model fails, and that tells you where to focus the next round of human effort.

I don't think humans go away in this picture at all. I think they become more valuable, because their time is spent on the decisions that actually move model performance. The transition is less about a single new tool and more about a mindset change: treating annotation as part of a continuous, data-centric development loop instead of a one-time outsourced step before training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I say annotation 2.0, I'm really contrasting it with what I'd call annotation 1.0, which is the paradigm most of us grew up with in this field. You collect a big pile of data, you hand it off to a team of human labelers, often somewhere far away from the actual problem, they draw boxes or assign class labels according to a spec, and then the data comes back and you train a model. It's linear, it's labor-intensive, and honestly the data and the model never really talk to each other. The annotation happens in a vacuum.

Annotation 2.0, the way I think about it, is fundamentally a shift from annotation as a one-time labor task to annotation as a continuous, model-in-the-loop, data-centric process. A few things change. First, the model becomes a first-class participant. You've got foundation models and your own task models that can pre-label, propose, or flag uncertain examples, so the human's job moves from drawing every box to verifying, correcting, and deciding what matters. The human is doing the high-value cognitive work rather than the repetitive mechanical work.

Second, the unit of attention shifts from the individual sample to the dataset as a whole. Instead of asking "is this label right," you start asking "where is my dataset weak, where are the duplicates, where are the mislabeled or ambiguous examples, which slices is the model failing on." Annotation becomes a way to intervene on the data distribution, not just to fill in missing fields.

And third, it's iterative. You label a little, you train, you look at the failures, you go back and label the things that will actually move the model. That tight loop is where I think most of the leverage is.

Now, in terms of the transition itself, I don't think it's going to be a flip of a switch. I think it happens in stages. The first stage, which we're already deep into, is just using models to accelerate the existing workflow. Pre-labeling, smart tools, that kind of thing. It's annotation 1.0 with a turbocharger. The second stage is when teams start to actually instrument their data, when they have tooling that lets them inspect, query, and curate what they've got, and the labeling budget starts getting allocated based on evidence rather than on just labeling everything. And the third stage, which is where I think things get really interesting, is when annotation becomes almost indistinguishable from model development. You're spending most of your time in the data, and the model is a lens you're using to understand it.

The cultural shift is honestly the hardest part. For a long time, data work was seen as the unglamorous thing you outsourced so you could get to the fun part, the modeling. Annotation 2.0 asks engineers and scientists to treat the data as the primary artifact they're engineering. That takes new tooling, sure, but it also takes a mindset change, and in my experience the mindset change is what actually determines whether a team gets there.

astra-6.text:
I think the transition is from people producing every annotation by hand to people guiding and correcting a system that does more of that work. Today, the basic interaction is often, “Here’s an image; draw a box around the object.” With annotation 2.0, the interaction becomes, “Here’s what the model thinks is in the image. Is it right, and if it’s wrong, what do we need to teach it?”

That creates a feedback loop. The model helps with annotation, the person supplies judgment where it matters, and those corrections improve the model. The interesting challenge is deciding when to involve the person. You don’t want someone repeatedly confirming things the system already handles well; you want their attention on examples that reveal a gap.

I see that happening incrementally. We’ll still need human expertise, but the tools should let that expertise go further. Success isn’t simply drawing boxes faster. It’s getting to a model that works with less repetitive human effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the transition is from treating annotation as a separate task—where you collect a dataset, send it off to be labeled, and then train a model—to treating it as an ongoing collaboration between people and models. The model can do some of the work, and the person can focus on correcting mistakes, resolving ambiguity, and providing the information the model actually needs.

That changes the question from “How do I label a million images?” to “What should I ask a person to do next to improve this system?” Sometimes that might be drawing a box. Sometimes it might be verifying a prediction or giving a higher-level description of what’s happening.

I don’t see that happening overnight. We’ll move toward it as the tools make that feedback loop easier and as people become comfortable measuring progress by how much the model improves, rather than simply how many annotations they’ve collected.
